brief.topic: Better in Every Group, Worse Overall?

s01: Team A does better on easy tasks.
It also does better on hard tasks.
Could team B still have the better overall success rate?
These are invented numbers.
On easy tasks, A succeeds nine times out of ten: ninety percent.
B succeeds eighty times out of one hundred: eighty percent.
On hard tasks, A succeeds twenty times out of one hundred: twenty percent.
B succeeds once out of ten: ten percent.
A leads in both groups.
Now put the groups together.
A has twenty nine successes in one hundred ten attempts.
About twenty six percent.
B has eighty one successes in one hundred ten attempts.
About seventy four percent.
The ranking reverses.
The key is the mixture.
A did mostly hard tasks.
B did mostly easy tasks.
An overall rate weights each group by how many attempts it contains.
It is not the simple average of the two percentages.
Give both teams the same mixture instead: half easy, half hard.
A's weighted rate becomes fifty five percent.
B's becomes forty five percent.
The reversal disappears.
This is Simpson's paradox.
Before comparing a single percentage, look at what went into it.
These totals alone cannot tell us what caused the difference.

scenes.narration:
Team A does better on easy tasks. It also does better on hard tasks. Could team B still have the better overall success rate?

These are invented numbers. On easy tasks, A succeeds nine times out of ten: ninety percent. B succeeds eighty times out of one hundred: eighty percent.

On hard tasks, A succeeds twenty times out of one hundred: twenty percent. B succeeds once out of ten: ten percent. A leads in both groups.

Now put the groups together. A has twenty nine successes in one hundred ten attempts. About twenty six percent. B has eighty one successes in one hundred ten attempts. About seventy four percent. The ranking reverses.

The key is the mixture. A did mostly hard tasks. B did mostly easy tasks. An overall rate weights each group by how many attempts it contains. It is not the simple average of the two percentages.

Give both teams the same mixture instead: half easy, half hard. A's weighted rate becomes fifty five percent. B's becomes forty five percent. The reversal disappears.

This is Simpson's paradox. Before comparing a single percentage, look at what went into it. These totals alone cannot tell us what caused the difference.
